sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Post-Onion is a participatory, dialogue-based performance that took place in a gallery and a theater black box.
The performance space was pre-designed: the audience would enter a hall where the floor was covered with a white cloth.
At the end of the hall, a large pot was placed on a red circle.
Three empty chairs were placed around the pot, and several onions were scattered around it.
At the beginning of the performance, three performers would sit on the chairs and begin chopping the onions inside the pot with knives.
Throughout the performance, the smell of onions spread across the entire space, irritating all attendees.
This action, simultaneous with the dialogue, was an inseparable part of the performance experience.
After a few moments, the performance designer would explain to the audience that a dialogue was going to be formed around a topic in this performance, and rules were established for this discussion.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The project was performed in a gallery and a black box theater space.
The selection of this space was made to create an atmosphere different from the traditional/known function of art galleries, which are usually based on exhibition, sales, and the art market.
The space was defined in a way to change the audience's perception of looking at artworks and to facilitate the possibility of active participation and dialogue.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: The main motivation for the project was the necessity of dialogue in a closed society and the transfer of ideas under the pretext of an artwork.

The project sought to create a platform, however temporary, for dialogue and the exchange of views; a space that is less feasible in official art platforms due to the over-commercialization/commodification of art.

From the artist's perspective, the lack of a space for dialogue and exchange of ideas within the art context was one of the social and economic backbones that influenced the formation of this project.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The most significant obstacle in executing the project was the administrative complexities and the necessity of obtaining permits from authorities to perform any cultural programs.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: Ahmadali Kargaran (born 1973, Bandar Abbas) is a multidisciplinary artist whose works, while paying special attention to the environment, are often inspired by the nature and indigenous culture of his habitat.
Alongside painting in his studio, Ahmad focuses on site-specific art installations, especially in public spaces, as well as performance art.
He has actively participated in the art scene of Hormuz Island since the 2000s.
Over these years, he has worked as the art director of the Jerry Pollock’s Residence and as the supervisor for various art events and festivals.
Social Media: @ahmadkargaran
Website: https://www.google.com/search?q=ak.blogsky.com
The rules of the dialogue were defined as follows:
Anyone could participate in the dialogue.
Anyone who wanted to express their opinion had to eliminate one of the three people present and take their place on one of the chairs around the pot.
The person who was speaking was obliged to chop onions at the same time.
Every individual could change the topic of the dialogue and have the group engage with their proposed topic.
After explaining the rules, the performance designer presented his proposed topic.
He spoke about the experience of burying one of his friends and how, at that time, someone had asked his opinion about life after death and the existence of God.
He shared his answer in detail with the audience and asked the other performers to express their views.
After one of the performers shared their opinion, a volunteer who wanted to participate in the discussion was invited to join the group, choose one of the three people, and take their seat.
This rotation continued in the same manner, and the composition of the individuals around the pot constantly changed.
During the performance, the dialogue took on various forms.
After the first rounds of people who spoke in line with the topic of death and its philosophy, some individuals requested a change of topic upon entering.

These topic changes were limited and included subjects such as the role of the audience in contemporary art, audience-centric approach, the concerns of the nineties generation, and social networks like Instagram and Facebook.
At the same time, a few people tried to adopt a type of deconstructive behavior upon entering.
One individual jumped on a chair and announced that instead of the proposed topics, he would like to talk about his friend.
In the course of the performance, all three original performers were quickly removed from the chairs.
The performance designer did not return to his chair, but one person returned to the chair multiple times and demanded to be present again.
Alongside these situations, some individuals attempted to make an anarchistic entry into the dialogue.
Additionally, a few people made the performance itself the subject of discussion and critique during the event.
Despite all these shifts, the main topic of the dialogue—albeit in a fragmented manner—was pursued until the end.
Some audience members stayed in the hall until the end, while a large number gradually left the hall.
